headline: Nvidia scandal hits Trump’s political vulnerabilities after Democratic sweep
author: Isaac Arnsdorf, Cat Zakrzewski

paragraphs.text: Sex. Money. Power. Espionage. As Washington scandals go, this one has everything.

But what really makes ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy an explosive political problem for the White House is that it brings together the very issues that propelled Democrats to their largest congressional majority since 1990. Voters revolted against President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, with widespread concerns about artificial intelligence, data centers, competition from China, and special access and favors for billionaires.

Those concerns vaulted the Nvidia scandal atop Democrats’ list for investigating the Trump administration, according to Rep. Stephen F. Lynch (D-Massachusetts), a member of the House Financial Services and Oversight committees. The latter panel will focus on national security dangers, including why Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick declined to blacklist companies suspected of smuggling advanced chips to China made by Nvidia, whose processors power much of the AI industry, and why Trump continued to talk to Huang and bring him on Air Force One.
“We really want to get to the bottom of this,” Lynch said, noting Nvidia committed $25 million for Trump’s White House ballroom. “Was there some type of quid pro quo there?”

The scandal is engulfing Washington as Trump prepares to travel to China next week and meet with its president, Xi Jinping. A senior U.S. official said Trump is unlikely to raise the Huang subject with his Chinese counterpart.
“The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip,” said the official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly.

Huang will not join this trip. On the last visit to China in May, Trump picked up Huang on Air Force One in Alaska, despite a warning from Secretary of State and national security adviser Marco Rubio that the U.S. had obtained intelligence that showed Huang was having an affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

Concerns over the national security and economic fallout are not limited to Democrats. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott (R-South Carolina) asked Huang and Lutnick to testify, and House Republicans are demanding Huang come in for a transcribed interview, threatening him with a subpoena. The top Republican and Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee also asked Lutnick for a classified briefing.

“If you’re in bed with a Chinese spy and you’re an individual with top-secret clearances developing these things related to everything from military tech to AI across the board to data crunching and everything else, this is a very big concern,” said Brian Mast (R-Florida), the House Foreign Affairs Committee chairman who signed the letter to Huang along with House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar (R-Michigan) and House Intelligence Committee Chairman Rick Crawford (R-Arkansas). “It’s painful to see this happen to Nvidia because they are one of the most important American tech companies, probably the most American tech company right now.”
The Foreign Affairs Committee’s ranking Democrat, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, who is seeking the gavel when Democrats take the majority in January, said he hopes the probe can be bipartisan.

“We’ve seen the tip of the iceberg,” he told reporters inside the U.S. Capitol on Thursday. “We need to know whether or not the Chinese government got any additional information, what information it was, how much, and then who knew what when.”
Trump has said little publicly on the scandal this week except to sympathize with Huang.
“I always thought of him as a fine man,” Trump said in an interview on Thursday with Stephen A. Smith, noting that he spoke with Huang the day before. “He’s going through hell.”

Others in the administration have pointed the finger at Lutnick, whose department is responsible for restricting exports of sensitive technology. “Commerce has the pen,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on CNBC on Friday. Last week, Bessent confronted Lutnick over why he hadn’t taken action despite directions from Trump on three occasions, according to a former administration official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe a private conversation.
Lutnick agreed to appear voluntarily before Scott’s Banking Committee, a Commerce Department spokeswoman said.
Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) said he would like to question Lutnick on why he allowed the sale of advance chips to the company of the suspected spy that Huang was having an affair with.
“Congress is not going to let this go,” he said.

In a sign of how the political winds have shifted since Nov. 3, Nvidia is counting on an experienced Democrat to help manage the crisis. In June, the company brought on Bruce Andrews, a former Commerce Department official in the Obama administration.

In the midterms, 56 percent of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress, and two-thirds of them voted for Democrats, according to the broadcast networks’ exit polls. Ninety percent said corruption was a crucial or major factor, and they favored Democrats to Republicans, 58 percent to 40 percent.

“Tech accountability was a winning message at the ballot box because of the AI industry’s cozy and corrupt relationship with Trump. Now we are learning Big Tech’s wrongdoing went far beyond corruption,” said Sacha Haworth, founder of the Tech Oversight Project, a watchdog group advising Democrats. “We want to see a Democratic Congress investigate Nvidia for anticompetitive practices that pass off costs to consumers, what the company knew about chip smuggling operations with China, and what Nvidia received in exchange for donations to the Trump campaign and ballroom.”
Some of those themes have crossover appeal to China hawks and tech critics within Trump’s coalition.

“This is going to end in tears unless we get some very smart people to start saying, ‘Hey, what is in the country’s interest?’” former White House strategist Stephen K. Bannon said on his influential online talk show on Friday. “Not the oligarchs. Not the stock market. … This goes to the beating heart of the modern world economy and who’s actually in charge.”
Mariana Alfaro, Jarrell Dillard, Noah Robertson and Nancy Cook contributed reporting.
